Alternative 6: If the present authority under the Endangered Species Act of 1969 were repealed, efforts for restoration of most species would collapse. Efforts for some species largely supported by other agencies outside the Interior might continue, but coordinated effort within the Department of the Interior would fail. An estimated 10 species would become extinct within 10 years and possibly 25 or 30 species in 20 years. Tenure of the remainder would be considerably shortened.
Alternatives 2, 5, and 6, would be particularly destructive of the welfare of endangered species and would lead to extinction of some species. This would save millions of dollars of government funds, particularly for land acquisition and for management of these lands later. It would allow continued economic development of these lands and permit many government and private construction projects to go forth without costly alterations—projects which involve real estate developments, highways, water developments, agriculture, industry, etc.. Some future projects of this type would not even be possible with consideration being given endangered species.
As opposed to these negative impacts, the American public has expressed deep appreciation for wildlife--they enjoy seeing it or simply knowing it is there. A big market for television programs, motion pictures, and books on willdife has developed. Rare or unusual species are prime attractions. Many people feel a moral obligation to prevent the extinction of any form, especially ones which might play important roles in ecosystems now or in the future. Preserving an endangered species saves not only the species itself but in many instances an entire habitat type or ecosystem. This in turn means saving areas in a natural state for aesthetic, cultural, scientific, and educational values.
